planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, near-neutral soil in full sun; this wild Korean species is the taxonomic parent of popular dwarf lilac selections but is rarely sold itself, so seed-grown plants will show more variation in size and bloom timing than named clones.

directions: Set out bare-root or container plants in full sun and well-drained soil, spacing them to allow for a rounded, multi-stemmed shrub form at maturity. This species blooms two to three weeks after common lilac, carrying dense upright panicles of fragrant pale lavender-pink flowers on a naturally tidy, compact frame without the legginess common lilac can develop. Give it a real winter chill period for reliable flowering, and prune only lightly right after bloom since flower buds form on the previous year's wood.

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in full sun in average, well-drained soil; this extremely cold-hardy northern Chinese species is widely used in shelterbelt and conservation plantings and tolerates heavier, less fertile soils better than most garden lilac hybrids.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil with reasonable air circulation, since the dense foliage of this stout shrub can hold moisture and invite powdery mildew in humid climates. Flowering a full two to three weeks after common lilac, it extends the lilac season with upright clusters of pink to lilac-pink flowers held above glossy, deeply veined leaves. It is one of the parent species behind the cold-hardy Preston hybrid lilacs and is itself valued more for extreme winter toughness and dense screening habit than for fragrance.

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in full sun in well-drained soil; this far-eastern Russian/Korean/Manchurian species is among the most cold-tolerant lilacs available and is favored for shelterbelt and prairie windbreak plantings in extreme climates.

directions: Site in full sun with well-drained soil, allowing room for a large, vigorous, upright-oval shrub that can reach small-tree proportions over time. Narrow, tapering leaflet-like leaves and long, loose panicles of violet-purple flowers appear after common lilac has finished, extending bloom season into early summer. Grown far more for its exceptional hardiness and vigor in harsh continental climates than for fragrance or showiness, it is a workhorse species for windbreaks and large-scale screening rather than a refined specimen shrub.

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in full sun to light shade in well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil; this western Chinese species has finer, more delicate foliage and panicles than common lilac and benefits from some shelter from harsh drying winds.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, giving this airy western Chinese species room to develop its characteristically loose, open, arching habit rather than the dense mass typical of common lilac. Slender panicles of pale pink flowers dangle from the branch tips in late spring, carrying a strong, sweet fragrance that has made selections of this species popular with lilac collectors seeking something more graceful than the usual garden hybrids. Its fine-textured, narrow leaves and relatively open growth also make it easier to underplant than bulkier lilac species.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in full sun to light shade in well-drained soil; this is the earliest-blooming deutzia species in general cultivation, so siting it where late frosts rarely reach open flowers protects the display.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, where this compact Chinese species produces pure white flowers singly or in small loose clusters along arching branches before most other deutzias have even leafed out. Its earlier bloom time than D. scabra or D. gracilis makes it useful for extending the deutzia season into early spring, pairing well with late-flowering bulbs. After bloom, thin out a portion of the oldest canes at ground level every few years to keep the mounded habit from becoming congested.

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in full sun to light shade in well-drained soil; this Yunnan/Sichuan species was among E.H. Wilson's early-20th-century Chinese introductions and is now mostly found through specialty shrub nurseries and collectors rather than mainstream garden centers.

directions: Site in full sun to light shade in well-drained soil, where this western Chinese mock orange produces intensely fragrant white flowers marked with a distinctive purple-maroon stain at the base of the petals and around the calyx, a trait that distinguishes it at a glance from plain-white mock orange species. Bloom comes in early summer on arching branches, and like other philadelphus the richest scent carries on warm, still evenings. Prune immediately after flowering, removing a portion of the oldest wood at the base, since flowers form on the previous season's growth.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs
